Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We get asymptotics for the volume of large balls in an arbitrary locally compact group G with polynomial growth. This is done via a study of the geometry of G and a generalization of P. Pansu's thesis. In particular, we show that any such G is weakly commensurable to some simply connected solvable Lie group S, the Lie shadow of G. We also show that large balls in G have an asymptotic shape, i.e. after a suitable renormalization, they converge to a limiting compact set which can be interpreted geometrically. We then discuss the speed of convergence, treat some examples and give an application to ergodic theory. We also answer a question of Burago about left invariant metrics and recover some results of Stoll on the irrationality of growth series of nilpotent groups.

outputs.L1: We derive asymptotic estimates for the volume of large balls in an arbitrary locally compact group \(G\) of polynomial growth by studying the geometry of \(G\) and generalizing P. Pansu’s thesis. In particular, we show that every such group \(G\) is weakly commensurable with a simply connected solvable Lie group \(S\), called the Lie shadow of \(G\). We further establish that large balls in \(G\) have an asymptotic shape: after suitable renormalization, they converge to a limiting compact set that admits a geometric interpretation. We then examine the rate of convergence, discuss several examples, and present an application to ergodic theory. Finally, we answer a question of Burago concerning left-invariant metrics and recover several results of Stoll on the irrationality of growth series of nilpotent groups.
outputs.L2: We determine the asymptotic behavior of the volumes of large balls in every locally compact group \(G\) of polynomial growth. Our approach analyzes the geometry of \(G\) and extends the work developed in P. Pansu’s thesis. In particular, we prove that \(G\) is weakly commensurable with a simply connected solvable Lie group \(S\), referred to as the Lie shadow of \(G\). We further establish that, under an appropriate rescaling, large balls in \(G\) approach a geometrically meaningful compact limiting set. We examine the rate of this convergence, present several examples, and derive an application in ergodic theory. Finally, we resolve a question posed by Burago concerning left-invariant metrics and rederive certain results of Stoll on the irrationality of growth series for nilpotent groups.

This work derives precise asymptotic formulas for the volume of large balls in arbitrary locally compact groups of polynomial growth. Extending the ideas developed in Pansu’s thesis, it provides a broad analysis of the large-scale geometry of these groups beyond the classical setting of finitely generated nilpotent groups.

A central structural result shows that every locally compact group of polynomial growth is weakly commensurable with a simply connected solvable Lie group, referred to as its **Lie shadow**. This Lie-theoretic model captures the group’s asymptotic geometry and makes it possible to study volume growth through more explicit geometric and algebraic methods.

Within this framework, the work proves an asymptotic shape theorem: after applying a suitable renormalization, large metric balls converge to a compact limiting set with a clear geometric interpretation. This convergence yields the leading asymptotics of ball volumes and clarifies how the algebraic structure of the group determines its geometry at large scales.

The analysis also addresses rates of convergence and presents examples illustrating the range and limitations of the general theory. In addition, the results are applied to questions in ergodic theory, provide an answer to a question of Burago concerning left-invariant metrics, and recover Stoll’s results on the irrationality of growth series for nilpotent groups. Altogether, the work offers a unified geometric and Lie-theoretic account of asymptotic volume growth in locally compact groups of polynomial growth.
outputs.L4:
This work develops a general asymptotic theory for the volume and geometry of large balls in arbitrary locally compact groups of polynomial growth. Extending Pansu’s methods beyond finitely generated nilpotent groups, it shows that every such group can be related, up to compact factors and weak commensurability, to a connected, simply connected solvable Lie group called its **Lie shadow**. Passing to the nilshadow and then to the associated graded nilpotent Lie group produces a canonical asymptotic model equipped with a homogeneous left-invariant sub-Finsler metric.

For any proper, locally bounded, left-invariant metric—or, more generally, an appropriate periodic pseudodistance—the metric balls become asymptotically equivalent, after rescaling, to the unit ball of this homogeneous metric. Thus the rescaled spaces converge in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense to a graded nilpotent Lie group, and the rescaled balls converge to a compact, geometrically meaningful limit shape. If \(\mu\) is Haar measure and \(D\) is the homogeneous dimension of the asymptotic nilpotent model, one obtains
\[
\mu(B(t))\sim c\,t^{D}
\qquad (t\to\infty),
\]
where \(c>0\) is the Haar volume of the limiting unit ball, with the appropriate normalization. This establishes the existence of an exact leading term for volume growth rather than merely upper and lower polynomial bounds.

The approach also provides quantitative comparisons between the original metric and its asymptotic model, yielding estimates for the rate at which balls approach their limit shape and for the error in the volume asymptotics. Because large balls form well-controlled Følner families, these geometric results have applications to ergodic theory, including averaging and pointwise ergodic statements along metric balls. They also clarify the large-scale behavior of left-invariant Riemannian, sub-Riemannian, word, and other periodic metrics, showing that their asymptotic geometry is governed by a homogeneous sub-Finsler structure on the associated graded group.

Finally, the volume asymptotics connect geometric growth with algebraic and combinatorial properties of finitely generated nilpotent groups. In particular, the structure of the leading growth constant and the precision of the asymptotic expansion can be used to derive irrationality results and obstructions to rationality for growth series associated with suitable generating sets. Overall, the work supplies a unified geometric framework for understanding large balls, asymptotic cones, volume growth, and growth series throughout the full class of locally compact groups of polynomial growth.
outputs.L5:
### Pansu Differentiation and Lie Groups

Pansu differentiation is a fundamental concept in the study of Carnot groups, a special class of nilpotent Lie groups equipped with a natural geometric structure. Introduced by Pierre Pansu, it generalizes the classical derivative to spaces whose geometry is anisotropic and often non-Euclidean.

This derivative respects both the group operation and the family of dilations associated with a Carnot group. Instead of being represented by an ordinary linear map, the Pansu derivative is a homogeneous Lie group homomorphism. It therefore captures the algebraic and geometric behavior of mappings more accurately than standard differentiation.

Pansu’s theory has important applications in geometric group theory, sub-Riemannian geometry, and analysis on metric spaces. In particular, it helps researchers understand the rigidity of mappings between Lie groups and the large-scale geometry of negatively curved spaces.

We study the large-scale geometry of balls in compactly generated locally compact groups of polynomial growth. For metrics induced by compact generating sets, we establish asymptotic volume laws of the form
\[
\mu(B(r))\sim c\,r^{D},
\]
where \(D\) is the homogeneous dimension of the associated graded nilpotent group. After rescaling, the balls converge to the unit ball of a left-invariant sub-Finsler metric on the asymptotic cone, yielding a canonical limit shape. counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a mathematical article that generalizes Pansu’s thesis using Lie shadows, studies convergence rates, and applies the findings to ergodic theory and growth series.
counterfactuals.output:
The article extends Pansu’s asymptotic-geometry theorem from finitely generated nilpotent groups to general locally compact groups of polynomial growth.

Its main results are:

- **Lie-shadow reduction.** A polynomial-growth group is modeled at large scale by a simply connected solvable Lie group—its **Lie shadow**—and ultimately by an associated graded nilpotent Lie group.
- **Limit shape theorem.** After rescaling, any suitable periodic metric, including word metrics, converges to a homogeneous sub-Finsler metric on this graded group. Thus large metric balls converge to a canonical compact “limit shape,” and distances are asymptotically equivalent to the limiting Carnot–Carathéodory distance.
- **Volume growth.** The theorem recovers the Bass–Guivarc’h homogeneous dimension and gives precise asymptotics
  \[
  \operatorname{vol} B(t)\sim c\,t^{D},
  \]
  with \(D\) determined by the graded Lie algebra.
- **Quantitative convergence.** The paper obtains bounds on how quickly rescaled metrics and balls approach their asymptotic shapes. The rates are polynomial and depend on the nilpotency structure, with stronger estimates in low-step cases. These also yield error terms for ball-volume and lattice-point asymptotics.
- **Ergodic-theoretic consequences.** Large balls form asymptotically regular/Følner averaging sets. This supports ergodic theorems for averages over metric balls and, in random or cocycle settings, deterministic asymptotic norms and limit shapes.
- **Growth-series consequences.** The volume asymptotics and their error terms control the coefficients and singular behavior of growth series near their dominant singularity, giving restrictions on—and in special cases information about—their rationality or analytic form.

Conceptually, the article shows that the large-scale geometry of every polynomial-growth group is governed by a homogeneous nilpotent model, while the quantitative results explain how rapidly the original discrete or non-nilpotent geometry becomes indistinguishable from that model.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an academic abstract explaining how arbitrary locally compact groups with polynomial growth are weakly commensurable to simply connected solvable Lie groups and how their rescaled balls converge to a limiting shape.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** We describe the large-scale geometry of compactly generated locally compact groups of polynomial growth. Using the structure theory of such groups, we show that, after quotienting by a compact normal subgroup and passing to a cocompact closed subgroup, every such group admits a proper cocompact homomorphism into a simply connected solvable Lie group of polynomial growth. Thus, in the coarse sense generated by compact extensions, cocompact inclusions, and proper cocompact homomorphisms, the original group is weakly commensurable to a solvable Lie model. This reduction preserves word-metric geometry up to quasi-isometry and permits the application of nilshadow and asymptotic-cone techniques. For any compact generating set—or, more generally, any periodic adapted metric—the associated metric balls, rescaled by their radius, converge in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense to the unit ball of a left-invariant sub-Finsler metric on the graded nilpotent Lie group associated with the Lie model. Equivalently, after suitable asymptotic coordinates, the rescaled balls converge in Hausdorff distance to a compact limiting shape. The limit is determined by the asymptotic norm induced on the first layer of the graded Lie algebra, while compact factors and non-nilpotent rotational components disappear under scaling. This provides a unified Lie-theoretic description of both the weak commensurability class and the asymptotic shape of arbitrary locally compact groups of polynomial growth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: What are the principal contributions of a paper on the large-scale geometry of locally compact groups, including Burago’s question about left-invariant metrics and Stoll’s results on irrational growth series?
counterfactuals.output:
The paper develops a general framework for studying locally compact groups through proper left-invariant—or more generally periodic—metrics at large scale. Its main contributions are:

- **A metric model for polynomial-growth groups.** For a compactly generated locally compact group of polynomial growth, the large-scale geometry is described by a graded nilpotent Lie group, often called the graded nilshadow, equipped with a left-invariant sub-Finsler/Carnot–Carathéodory metric.

- **Asymptotic shape of metric balls.** After rescaling, balls for word metrics and other periodic metrics converge to the unit ball of this limiting sub-Finsler metric. This extends Pansu’s asymptotic-cone theorem beyond finitely generated nilpotent groups.

- **A broad form of Burago’s periodic-metric theorem.** Burago showed in the abelian setting that a periodic metric is asymptotic to a norm. The paper extends this principle to groups of polynomial growth: the norm is replaced by a homogeneous sub-Finsler metric on the associated graded nilpotent group. It also clarifies that asymptotic equivalence—an error \(o(d)\)—is the natural general statement; a uniformly bounded additive error requires stronger assumptions and can fail in nonabelian settings.

- **Growth and volume asymptotics.** The geometric limit yields precise polynomial growth laws for large balls, identifies the leading growth constant with the Haar volume of the limiting unit ball, and provides estimates on the discrepancy between discrete balls and their continuous limit shapes.

- **Connections with Stoll’s growth-series results.** Applying these metric and lattice-point estimates to nilpotent groups, especially Heisenberg-type examples, recovers and extends phenomena found by Stoll: growth series need not be rational and, for suitable generating sets or groups, can be irrational or transcendental. The geometry of the limiting sub-Finsler ball explains why rational growth behavior should not be expected in general.

Overall, the paper unifies asymptotic cones, periodic metrics, nilpotent approximation, volume growth, and algebraic properties of growth series within one large-scale geometric theory for locally compact groups.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a short research overview of asymptotic ball volumes in polynomial-growth groups, mentioning Lie shadows, asymptotic shapes, speed of convergence, examples, and applications.
counterfactuals.output:
For a finitely generated group \(G\) with finite generating set \(S\), let \(B_S(n)\) be the word-metric ball of radius \(n\). Gromov’s theorem says that polynomial growth is equivalent to \(G\) being virtually nilpotent. If \(N\leq G\) is a finite-index nilpotent subgroup, its lower central series determines the **Bass–Guivarc’h dimension**
\[
D=\sum_{i\ge 1} i\,\mathrm{rank}(N_i/N_{i+1}),
\]
and
\[
|B_S(n)|\sim c_S n^D
\]
for a positive constant \(c_S\).

The geometric explanation uses a **Lie shadow**: one embeds \(N\) as a lattice in its Mal’cev completion and then passes to the associated graded, or “nilshadow,” a Carnot group. Pansu’s scaling theorem identifies the rescaled word metrics with a left-invariant sub-Finsler Carnot–Carathéodory metric. Thus \(n^{-1}B_S(n)\) converges to a compact **asymptotic shape**, namely the unit ball of this limiting metric, and \(c_S\) is its Haar volume after lattice normalization.

The **speed of convergence** is subtler. General theory gives \(o(n^D)\) error in ball volume, while quantitative results provide power-type bounds in many nilpotent settings; exponents depend on nilpotency step, metric approximation, and lattice-point counting near the limit boundary. Sharp second-order terms are known only in special cases, and nonsmooth sub-Finsler spheres can create substantial arithmetic and geometric complications.

Basic examples include:

- \(G=\mathbb Z^d\): the limit shape is the convex hull of the generators, and ball counts are governed by Ehrhart-type lattice-point asymptotics.
- The discrete Heisenberg group: \(D=4\), despite topological dimension \(3\); the limit is a sub-Finsler ball in the real Heisenberg Carnot group.
- Finite extensions of nilpotent groups: the same Lie-shadow picture persists, with constants adjusted by index and normalization.

These results support applications to random walks and heat kernels, Følner profiles and isoperimetry, harmonic analysis, lattice counting, geometric group theory, and quantitative versions of Gromov’s theorem. Key foundations are due to Bass, Guivarc’h, Gromov, Pansu, and later work on Lie shadows and quantitative convergence by Breuillard, Le Donne, and others.
